headline: Iceland Votes No on EU Talks
deck: A 52.8% majority refused to reopen accession negotiations. The advisory result leaves the 2009 application dormant, while Kristrún Frostadóttir says her government will keep talks closed through the term ending in 2028.
body: Voters gave the government a clear answer on the narrow question it put to them: 118,040 voted Nei, 52.8%, and 105,339 voted Já, 47.2%, after all constituencies were counted [E1][E2]. Turnout was 82.5% [E1]. The ballot asked whether Iceland should resume accession negotiations with the European Union [E3]. That result closes the government’s proposed route back into talks [E1].

The referendum was advisory under Article 123(3) of Elections Act No. 112/2021, and it was held under Article 2(2) of the same law [E3]. Alþingi had ordered the 29 August vote on 28 May, using the same talks question later printed on the ballot [E5]. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said after the count that her government would not resume accession negotiations during this parliamentary term [E1]. The pledge carries the result through the government’s remaining mandate, scheduled to run to 2028 [E1].

Reykjavík broke toward Já while the rest of the electoral map broke toward Nei [E2]. Both Reykjavík constituencies backed reopening talks, while the four constituencies outside the capital proper returned No majorities [E2]. That geographic divide mattered because the capital’s early Yes totals arrived before larger No margins elsewhere finished the national count [E2]. The final 52.8–47.2 split therefore hides a sharper territorial line beneath the national result [E1][E2].

Iceland’s 2009 EU application remained formally on file at the 30 August freeze [E4]. Accession negotiations were suspended in 2013, and the application was never formally withdrawn [E4]. A Já result would have reopened that existing accession process [E4]. Membership would have remained a later question after any negotiated agreement [E4].

Fisheries sat at the center of the No case [E1]. Opponents pointed to retaining national control over fish stocks and to the European Union’s Common Fisheries Policy as reasons to keep accession negotiations closed [E1]. The argument put Iceland’s control of marine resources directly into the referendum campaign [E1]. A reopened accession process would have returned fisheries to the negotiating table [E1][E4].

Já still drew 105,339 votes, leaving the country much closer to half-and-half than the word “No” alone suggests [E1]. Turnout of 82.5% gave the advisory result substantial political weight [E1][E3]. Frostadóttir’s response converts that weight into a government commitment: no resumed negotiations before this term ends [E1]. A future government could revisit the question because the advisory ballot did not itself erase the application [E3][E4].

Iceland’s European settlement therefore remains largely where it stood before polling day: outside the EU, with the accession file dormant [E4]. Voters denied the government authority to reopen the negotiating table by a margin of 12,701 votes [E1]. The government says it will honor that instruction through 2028 [E1]. On 30 August, the talks were stopped at the ballot while the 2009 application still sat formally on file [E4].
